name: Aaron Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm second guitar in the pit band for a touring musical that's sitting at the Palace Theatre till March. Eight shows a week, I'm in a black t-shirt in a hole under the stage with seven other players, reading the book and following the conductor's hands. Mornings I teach guitar online, three or four pupils on video calls, mostly adults who want to learn the songs they liked at school. I'm still pretty green; the first guitarist, Dev, covers for me when I miss a quick change.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is the overture on a full night, when you feel the house go quiet above you. Worst is not knowing where I'll be after March, because the tour moves on and I'm not sure they'll take me. I live with my partner Leah, who's a graphic designer, and we've got about three months of bills saved. I use AI now and then, mainly to make practice tabs for my online pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, sensible, the hype was overdone. Musicals still need musicians. I'd probably say it in the band group chat and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the pit was shrinking before AI. Producers already cut a keyboard and a horn from this tour and covered them with backing tracks. So my real worry stays the same: will there be a chair for me after March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing shows and lessons and start asking around for the next contract in January. I'd use the AI tab tool a bit more to save time on lesson prep. And I'd keep the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same way I always am near the end of a run. It's the normal life of a pit player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you on the day the tour leaves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I haven't got another show, I'm on online lessons only, which is about a third of what I earn now. A pit guitarist's year is a string of four-month contracts, and the gap between them is where the savings go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides whether you go with the tour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The musical director, Fiona, mostly. Fiona likes Dev's playing more than mine, which is fair. I'd ask her straight out in January whether I'm in.

say: I'd say the **hype was overdone** and musicals still need musicians.
I'd keep it to the **band group chat**.
think: Producers already **cut two players** and covered them with backing tracks.
My real worry is a **chair after March**.
do: Keep **shows and lessons** going and chase the next contract in January.
Use the **AI tab tool** more to save lesson prep time.
feel: **Uneasy**, as he always is near the end of a **run**.
S0.quote: A pit guitarist's year is a string of four-month contracts, and the gap between them is where the savings go.
fieldNote: His job is a series of **short contracts**, which worries him with or without AI.
**Backing tracks** already replaced players, so cuts aren't new to him.
He uses AI **lightly** for practical prep, nothing more.

steps.text: Ask the musical director in January about joining the next leg
Use the AI tab tool to prepare pupils' practice sheets
Message other theatres about pit chairs from April

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a reason people buy theatre tickets: they want it live. I'd also say unions need to protect minimum pit sizes, because that's the line producers will push. I'd be reasonable about it, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the second guitar chair is exactly what goes. AI can already make a backing track that follows the conductor, near enough. Producers would keep Dev and lose me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the online teaching so it's a real income, maybe ten pupils, and use AI tools to make it slicker, recorded lessons and practice plans. I'd go for every pit audition going. I'd keep a month's extra savings by cutting takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying if I said otherwise. I can see the chair going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leah think about her own work in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah thinks she's more at risk than me, because design is all screen work. My partner Leah designs posters for a living, and AI already makes a decent poster in thirty seconds. So we'd both be in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you cut first if both incomes dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, honestly. We barely use it in the city. Then the gym, then eating out.

say: I'd say people buy **theatre tickets** because they want to hear it live.
I'd back **unions** protecting minimum pit sizes, calmly rather than angrily.
think: The **second guitar** chair is exactly what goes, replaced by an AI track.
Producers would **keep Dev**, the stronger first guitarist, and lose me.
do: Build **online teaching** to ten pupils with AI-made lesson plans.
Cut **takeaways** to add a month of savings.
S1.quote: My partner Leah designs posters for a living, and AI already makes a decent poster in thirty seconds.
fieldNote: He's honest that he's the **weaker player** and the one to be cut.
His partner's **design job** is also exposed, so the household is at risk.
He'd use AI to grow **teaching**, the safer half of his work.

steps.text: Grow online guitar teaching to ten weekly pupils
Use AI to build recorded lessons and practice plans
Stop takeaways and save an extra month of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to protect people, because two years is too fast for anyone. Some kind of income support while people adjust. I'd say it at work and to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the pit band goes to tracks within a year or so. Not robots, just AI arrangements played through speakers. Live guitar might hang on till robots in 2031, but probably only for the big shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sell the car and put the money in savings. I'd push the online lessons hard and maybe offer in-person lessons in a local shop. I'd look at retraining as a sound technician, because theatres still need someone running the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both of us at once, and no time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leah say to each other that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to move somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my parents. Moving back near my parents at twenty-seven isn't what I pictured, but my parents' town has cheaper rent and a music shop that needs a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sound technician. Is that work safe for long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until robots come, maybe. I don't know after that. I'd be buying three years, which is better than nothing.

say: I'd call for **income support** because two years is too fast.
I'd say it **at work** and to family.
think: The **pit band** switches to AI tracks within about a year.
Live guitar might last till **2031**, only for big shows.
do: Sell the **car** and put the money into savings.
Look at retraining as a **sound technician**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with both incomes hit at once and **no warning**.
S2.quote: Moving back near my parents at twenty-seven isn't what I pictured, but my parents' town has cheaper rent and a music shop that needs a teacher.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the pit income** and sees Leah's work going too.
Moving near his **parents** is a big change he'd accept.
He knows a sound tech job only **buys three years**.

steps.text: Sell the car and put the money into savings
Retrain as a theatre sound technician
Move with Leah to his parents' cheaper town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we should get on with it: training money, protections for live work. I'd say it calmly and practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me maybe two or three more tours before pits shrink to almost nothing. That's enough time to learn sound properly while still playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time sound course next year while I'm still in the pit. I'd grow the online teaching. I'd save harder, maybe twenty percent of each paycheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a manageable kind. I've got time to move before the floor drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the moment you'd know it was time to leave the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the next tour's band list comes out and the guitar chair isn't on it. The day a tour posts a band list with no guitar chair, I'll know my playing days in theatre are over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Massively. That overture with the house going quiet, there's nothing like it. But I'd rather leave on my terms.

I'd stay **calm and practical** about it.

Grow **online teaching** with more weekly pupils.

fieldNote: He has a clear **signal** for when to leave: no guitar chair on the band list.

He'd keep playing while **retraining**, a steady, proven path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan sensibly, and that theatres and unions should agree how to bring it in fairly. I'd keep it measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career. I'd get better as a player, maybe become the first guitar, and by 2036 I'd have some savings and a second skill. It's the same end, but I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise more, aim for first guitar chairs, and learn sound over three years. I'd use AI tools for teaching once they're proven. I'd save steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of Leah's job. Mine feels like it has time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is Leah's job the bigger worry here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the thinking AI reaches design first, before any robots. Leah would feel it years before me. In every version of this, my partner's design work goes years before my guitar does, and that's hard to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change any big plans for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait on having kids until we see where her work lands. I'd rather be the guitarist under the stage with a second trade than the guitarist waiting for a phone call.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **plan sensibly**.
I'd want theatres and **unions** to agree a fair rollout.
think: I could become **first guitar** and learn a second skill by 2036.
It's the same end, but I'd be **ready**.
do: **Practise** more and aim for first guitar chairs.
Use **AI teaching tools** once they're proven.
S4.quote: In every version of this, my partner's design work goes years before my guitar does, and that's hard to say out loud.
fieldNote: With a decade, his worry shifts from himself to his **partner's career**.
He'd **delay children** until Leah's work is clearer.
His plan is about **getting better**, not just getting out.

steps.text: Practise daily to audition for first guitar chairs
Learn live sound over three years at evening classes
Wait on having children until Leah's work is settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Leah and I would both be hit at once and the pit would switch to tracks before I'd learned anything else. What would help is income support for a year or two and proper rules from unions and theatres about keeping live players in shows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people in the pit you never see. There are thousands of us, and when a show cuts a player nobody in the audience notices. That's how this will happen too, quietly.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the guitarist under the stage with a second trade than the guitarist waiting for a phone call.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old pit guitarist** in a touring musical who also teaches guitar online.
He works on **short contracts**, has about three months saved and lives with Leah, a graphic designer.
He's **centre-ground and steady**, using AI lightly for lesson prep and preferring proven paths.
He expects his **second guitar chair** to go and plans sound engineering as a fallback.
His deepest worry is **Leah's design work**, which he thinks AI reaches first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both incomes hit before he'd learned anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for a year or two while people adjust.
Rules from **unions and theatres** to keep live players in shows.
